summary: Explains how the CLUE protocol and its data channel are used together with existing signaling such as SIP and SDP to set up a telepresence call. It is an experimental document that ties the pieces of CLUE into a working call flow.

plainLanguage.summary: CLUE, Controlling Multiple Streams for Telepresence, lets the devices in a call choose which camera views they send and receive. It uses two separate negotiations: the session description settles which media streams can flow, and messages on a data channel settle which camera views exist and which ones each side wants.

subtitle: How a telepresence call agrees on which camera views each side sends and receives.

tldr.problem: A telepresence call needs more than one kind of agreement. The devices must sort out which media streams can be delivered where, and separately which camera views exist and which ones each side wants to receive.
tldr.mechanism: CLUE keeps those two negotiations apart. SDP, carried in SIP messages, negotiates the media streams and their limits. CLUE protocol messages, carried over a CLUE data channel, negotiate the Capture Sources and which of them are wanted. A CLUE group in the SDP ties the controlled media lines to that data channel.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines how a CLUE call is set up, how it can be upgraded from an ordinary call and taken back out of it mid-call, and how the two negotiations must behave when they disagree temporarily. It is an Experimental document.

today: RFC 8848 is an Experimental document and has not been obsoleted. It sits alongside the CLUE Framework in RFC 8845, the CLUE protocol in RFC 8847, and the data channel it uses in RFC 8850.

sections.title: Two Negotiations for One Call
sections.content:
CLUE, Controlling Multiple Streams for Telepresence, lets the devices in a telepresence call choose which camera views they send and receive. It does this with two separate negotiations that run at the same time. SDP, carried in SIP messages, negotiates the media capabilities that can be delivered to particular addresses on a device. CLUE protocol messages, carried over a CLUE data channel, negotiate which Capture Sources exist, what their attributes are, what constraints apply to them, and which Captures the far end wants to receive.

The split matters because the two carry different information. SDP defines media addresses and limits. The CLUE channel defines which Capture Devices are available, scene information and additional constraints. Because of that split, some operations cannot be done in one step. Advertising a new Capture that has a stream attached needs changes in both SDP and CLUE messaging.

Backwards compatibility is a first-class concern. A CLUE-capable device that calls a device without CLUE must be able to fall back to a working ordinary call. The RFC also defines how a call can be upgraded to CLUE part-way through, and how CLUE can be removed again mid-call to return to a standard call.
sections.plainLanguage: A telepresence call needs two kinds of agreement. One says which media streams can flow and where. The other says which camera views exist and which ones each side wants to receive. CLUE keeps them apart: the first uses SDP, the second uses messages on a data channel.

sections.title: The CLUE Group and the Data Channel
sections.content:
Two pieces of signalling announce CLUE support. The first is the sip.clue media feature tag, which a CLUE-capable device should include in its REGISTER requests and OPTIONS responses, and should also include in INVITE and UPDATE requests and responses. The presence of the tag in the contact field of a request or response shows that the far end supports CLUE. The second is the CLUE data channel, a bidirectional data channel used to carry CLUE messages inside an SCTP connection over DTLS. It must be established before any CLUE protocol message can be exchanged or any CLUE-controlled media can be sent.

The data channel is negotiated in SDP like any other data channel. A CLUE-capable device that wants CLUE must also include a CLUE group in its SDP Offer or Answer and put the mid value of the data channel's media line in that group. The group must name the mid of one and only one data channel. Only one CLUE group is specified, and a device must not include more than one unless it is following a specification that defines how several CLUE channels are signalled and it can either detect that the far end supports them or fail gracefully if it does not.

Each media line included in the CLUE group is controlled by that data channel. A media line is CLUE controlled when its mid value is in the group. Media lines outside the group follow the ordinary SDP rules for media streams. The RFC stresses that the restrictions on CLUE-controlled media apply even if the data channel negotiation failed, for any reason, or if the far end did not include the corresponding mid in its CLUE group.
sections.plainLanguage: Two things announce that a device supports CLUE. One is a tag in the SIP messages that says CLUE is available. The other is a data channel listed in the session description. The data channel and the media lines it controls are gathered in a group, so both ends know which streams CLUE is in charge of.

sections.title: How CLUE-Controlled Media Looks in SDP
sections.content:
The CLUE Framework defines Encodings, which represent what the sender is able to encode. Each Encoding that the Media Provider wishes to signal gets its own media line of the appropriate media type, marked sendonly or inactive. The usual SDP syntax then expresses the limits of the encoder, for example the format parameters for H.264.

Every media line representing a CLUE Encoding must carry a label attribute, and each label must be different from the labels of all the other media lines in the CLUE group. A dependent stream, such as a Forward Error Correction stream, must use the same label as the media line it depends on. The label is the reference used by the CLUE protocol. An advertisement message names the Encodings it offers by their labels, and a configure message names the Encoding to use for a particular Capture.

Until the Media Provider has received a valid CLUE configure message specifying the Capture to use for a stream, that stream must be treated as if its direction attribute were set to inactive. No RTP packets may be sent on it until the configuration is complete, while non-media packets such as STUN, RTCP and DTLS are still sent as their own specifications require.

A receiver that wants a CLUE stream in a particular Encoding signals that with a recvonly media line matching the sendonly one. Those lines are also CLUE controlled and must have their mid in the group, but they do not need a label, because only the labels of sendonly Encodings are referenced by CLUE messages.
sections.plainLanguage: Each camera view the sender can offer gets its own media line, and that line carries a short label. The CLUE messages use those labels to say which views are on offer and which one to use for a given camera. Until the receiver says which one to use, no video is sent on that line.

sections.title: The SDP Offer and Answer Procedure
sections.content:
A CLUE-capable device sending the first offer includes a media line for the CLUE data channel and a CLUE group holding the mid of that line. For interoperability with devices that do not support CLUE, it should not include any CLUE-controlled media lines beyond the data channel in the first offer, and it should include at least one ordinary media line. That recommendation is waived when the device has evidence that the far end is CLUE capable, for example because the INVITE carried the sip.clue tag.

In the answer, a CLUE-capable device that receives a data channel media line and a matching CLUE group should accept the data channel and put its mid in a corresponding CLUE group. If it receives a data channel line without a CLUE group, it may still accept the channel for other protocols, but CLUE must not be negotiated on it. Once both the offer and the answer contain a data channel media line whose mid is in the corresponding CLUE groups, CLUE has been negotiated and the call is CLUE enabled. If not, the call is not CLUE enabled, and CLUE-capable devices must either revert to ordinary behaviour or end the call.

The call can change afterwards. Further offer and answer exchanges may add CLUE-controlled media lines or activate and deactivate existing ones, and the devices should make sure that ordinary media of the same type is switched off once CLUE-controlled media of that type is working. A CLUE-capable device that receives an offer from a non-CLUE device should add a data channel media line and a CLUE group in a later offer, which turns the call into a CLUE-enabled one. A device that wants to disable CLUE during a call sends a new offer and answer, resets the stream sequence number of the CLUE channel, and must remove the CLUE group. If the data channel fails unexpectedly, the devices should keep the media flowing on the basis of the last negotiated CLUE messages until CLUE is re-established or disabled.

The RFC also covers multiplexing with the BUNDLE extension, which puts several media streams onto a single 5-tuple and so avoids opening many ports. Supporting BUNDLE is optional for a CLUE device. Because BUNDLE requires a unique address for each media line with a non-zero port in the first offer, a CLUE device that negotiates BUNDLE can avoid opening many ports, since it normally offers only the data channel at that stage.
sections.plainLanguage: The first offer lists the data channel and nothing else that CLUE controls, so a call to an ordinary device still works. When both ends accept the data channel and put it in the CLUE group, the call is CLUE enabled. The call can be upgraded to CLUE later, or taken back out of it, with further offers and answers.

sections.title: How the Two Negotiations Interact
sections.content:
The SDP and CLUE state machines run independently, on purpose. Interlocking them would risk invalid states if messages were lost or rewritten by middleboxes. The state of the CLUE channel does not restrict when a device may send a new SDP offer or answer, and the ability to send a CLUE advertisement or configure message is not restricted by the results or the state of the most recent SDP negotiation, unless that negotiation removed the CLUE channel.

One rule does bind the two together. CLUE-controlled media must not be sent unless it has been negotiated in both places: the most recent SDP exchange must contain an active media channel for that Encoding, and the device must have received a CLUE configure message specifying a valid Capture for it.

Because the two negotiations are separate, a device may receive an SDP offer naming a CLUE Encoding for which it has no Capture information yet, or a CLUE configure message for an Encoding that the far end has not yet put in SDP. A CLUE implementation must not reject a CLUE message just because some of its encoding identifiers do not match a label in SDP. Devices must cope with such mismatches, and must send updated SDP or CLUE messages as soon as they can so that the inconsistency is temporary. Because a new SDP negotiation costs more than a new CLUE message, a device that needs to change both should send the CLUE message first, so that the other side can answer with complete information.

The CLUE Framework also allows a Capture to be a composite of other Captures. A Media Provider sending switched media for such a Capture must include the CaptureID of the originating Capture in both RTP and RTCP, so the receiver knows which source it is looking at. Because that identifier arrives on a different path from the advertisement message that defines the composite, a receiver must not be disrupted when the two arrive in either order or disagree.
sections.plainLanguage: The two negotiations run side by side and neither waits for the other. The one rule that ties them together is that a video stream may only start once both the session description and the CLUE messages have agreed on it. When the two disagree for a moment, a device waits rather than failing.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
CLUE is built on other protocols, and the RFC says those should be secured by following the recommendations of each one. Using CLUE does add concerns of its own. A malicious party could subvert a CLUE-capable device and use it to attack a third party by driving large volumes of media, especially video, at that victim. A CLUE device can be told to send several media streams at once, which significantly increases the traffic directed at the victim.

The defence is receiver intent: the media recipient must intend to receive the packets. All CLUE-capable devices must therefore support key negotiation and receiver intent assurance using DTLS with SRTP on CLUE-controlled RTP media lines, and must use it or an equivalent mechanism. CLUE implementations may choose not to require SRTP for the older, non-CLUE-controlled media, for compatibility with older SIP clients that cannot support it.

The sip.clue media feature tag can be present even in calls that do not use CLUE, which adds to what can be learned about a device and can help an attacker fingerprint users from the set of features their device supports. For that reason, SIP signalling used to set up CLUE sessions should always be encrypted with TLS. The CLUE protocol also carries information that can help identify a particular user or the exact version of software in use, which the CLUE Framework document discusses.
sections.plainLanguage: Because CLUE can send several video streams at once, it must be sure the far end really wants them. All CLUE-controlled video must use DTLS with SRTP so the receiver proves it wants the media. The signalling that sets up a CLUE call should also be encrypted with TLS.
